explanations.explanation: True, baker. The song says, “…salvation is established as its walls and ramparts.” Walls made of salvation. My bakery walls can't even hold a calendar straight.

Not this time, friend. The song says the city has a strong wall, and the wall is salvation itself: “…salvation is established as its walls and ramparts.” So the statement on the card is True. Salvation is what stands around that city.

Yes, friend. The gates open for a righteous nation, “…one that remains faithful.” Remains is the word that counts there. That's the friend who actually returns your ladder, and every neighbor knows how rare that is.

Close the door on that one, baker. The song opens the gates for a righteous nation that remains faithful. A hidden guest at an open gate would be a strange party. Nobody could even find them to let them in.
Not proud, friend. The gates open for a nation that remains faithful. Proud sounds more like the lofty city in verse 5, and that one gets brought down to the ground, not welcomed in.

That's the one, baker. The song says God keeps the steadfast of mind in perfect peace, “…because he trusts in You.” The peace has a reason, and the reason is trust. It's not about how quiet life happens to be.

The song doesn't say that, friend. It gives one reason: “…because he trusts in You.” In fact, the same song talks about God's enemies in verse 11. So the peace comes from trust, not from a calm crowd.

Good thing that's not the reason, baker, or I'd be out. I once stamped a whole batch upside down and didn't notice until the first cookie came out smiling at me. The song gives a different reason: “…because he trusts in You.” Peace comes from trusting God, not from a spotless record.

explanations.answer: Because He is the Rock eternal
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. The song says, “…GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal.” My edges wore down, but a Rock eternal doesn't wear down at all. That's a reason worth leaning on.

explanations.answer: Because He gives His people riches
explanations.explanation: That's not in this song, friend. The reason it gives is that GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal. Riches never show up in these verses. The trust rests on who He is.

explanations.answer: Because He keeps His people from pain
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't promise that, baker. Look at verse 17, where the singers say they writhed and cried out in pain. The reason for trusting is the one in verse 4: “…GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal.” That Rock is there while the pain is happening.
That's it, baker. The song says the lofty city is trampled by “…the feet of the oppressed, the steps of the poor.” The ones who were pushed down are the ones walking over it. That's quite a turn.

Other way around, friend. The mighty aren't the ones doing the trampling in this verse. The song says it's “…the feet of the oppressed, the steps of the poor.” The lofty city is the one lying in the dust.

Not the wealthy, baker. The song names “…the feet of the oppressed, the steps of the poor.” The people stepping on that city are the ones with the least. The song doesn't give a single step to the wealthy.
Yes, baker. The singers say, “Your name and renown are the desire of our souls.” They aren't asking for a thing. They want Him. Now that's a wish list worth having.
Not that one, friend. The song opens by saying they already have a strong city. What the singers call the desire of their souls is His name and renown.

Close, but the song doesn't say that here, baker. Verse 8 says, “Your name and renown are the desire of our souls.” Enemies do come up a few verses later, but not as this desire. Their souls are set on God's name.

explanations.answer: The people of the world learn righteousness
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The song says, “…the people of the world learn righteousness.” When God's judgments come, the whole world gets a lesson. I only wish my cookie class went that well.

explanations.answer: The mountains of the world melt like wax
explanations.explanation: That picture is real, friend, but it's from another place. Psalm 97:5 says the mountains melt like wax before the LORD. Here in Isaiah the song says something different happens: “…the people of the world learn righteousness.”

explanations.answer: The rivers of the world turn to blood
explanations.explanation: That one belongs to Egypt, baker. Exodus 7:20 tells how the water of the Nile turned to blood there. This song says something else happens when God's judgments come: “…the people of the world learn righteousness.”
The song says the opposite, friend. “Though grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn righteousness.” Grace was shown, and he still didn't learn. So the answer is False.

That's right, baker. The song says, “Though grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn righteousness.” Grace comes his way and he still doesn't learn. I'd call that a very full plate that never got touched.

That's the one, baker. The song says the wicked man acts unjustly “…and fails to see the majesty of the LORD.” It's right there in front of him and he looks past it. That's like walking through my bakery and not noticing the ovens are on.
The poor do come up in verse 6, friend, but not here. What the wicked man doesn't see is “…the majesty of the LORD.” The song names the majesty of the LORD as what he misses.
A path does show up in this song, baker. Verse 7 says the path of the righteous is level. But what the wicked man doesn't see, in verse 10, is “…the majesty of the LORD.”
Yes, baker. The song says, “They will see Your zeal for Your people and be put to shame.” Zeal means He cares fiercely about His people. They don't see it yet, but the song says they will.
Not sorrow, friend. The song says the thing they will see is His zeal for His people. Sorrow doesn't show up in that verse at all.
Patience is a nice word, baker, but it's not the one in verse 11. The song says, “They will see Your zeal for Your people and be put to shame.” Zeal is the word that fits the blank.

That's it, baker. The singers say, “…all that we have accomplished, You have done for us.” They look at their whole list and hand the credit straight to Him. That's a good habit for any baker with a full cookie box.
No king gets the credit here, friend. The singers say, “…all that we have accomplished, You have done for us.” They're talking to the LORD when they say it.
No army in this verse, baker. The singers say, “…all that we have accomplished, You have done for us.” They aren't pointing to soldiers at all.
That's right, baker. The singers say, “…Your name alone do we confess.” Other lords have ruled over them, and still they confess only His name. That's one name on the whole list.
The song names those rulers as the other lords, friend. It says they ruled over the singers, but then it says, “…Your name alone do we confess.” The singers confess God's name, not the rulers'.
The fathers don't show up in this verse, baker. The singers say, “…Your name alone do we confess.” The only name they confess is the LORD's.

explanations.answer: All the borders of the land
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The song says, “…You have extended all the borders of the land.” He enlarged the nation, said it twice, and then stretched the borders out too. That's a lot of room to grow.
No Jerusalem in this verse, friend. The song says He extended “…all the borders of the land.” The walls aren't what gets stretched.

explanations.answer: All the days of their kings
explanations.explanation: Kings don't get extra days in this verse, baker. The song says, “…You have extended all the borders of the land.” It's the borders that get stretched, not the days.
That's the one, baker. The song says, “…when You disciplined them, they poured out a quiet prayer.” In their distress it came out soft. You don't need a big voice for this kind of prayer.
That's a real thing in Scripture, but it's not in this verse, friend. The song says what they poured out was “…a quiet prayer.” Their words were the thing being poured.
Loud is my department, baker, and this verse isn't it. The song says what they poured out was “…a quiet prayer.” Quiet, not loud.
Yes, baker. The singers say, “…we gave birth to wind.” All that pain, and nothing solid at the end. That's a rough picture, and I think they felt it.
Stone is heavy, friend, but it's not in the verse. The singers say, “…we gave birth to wind.” Nothing you could hold.
Fire does show up elsewhere in the song, baker, but not here. The singers say, “…we gave birth to wind.” So the pain ended in wind.
The song says the opposite, friend. “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise.” They don't stay in the dust. So the answer is False.
That's right, baker. The song says, “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise.” They don't stay in the dust. After all that wind, this is where the song turns.
That's it, baker. The song says, “Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust!” Dust doesn't get the last word here. It's a wake-up call with a tune attached.
That's not what the song says, friend. It calls out, “Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust!” Right here, the song is singing, not weeping.
Not rest, baker. The song tells those who dwell in the dust, “Awake and sing…” Waking up is the opposite of staying put.

explanations.answer: A little while until the wrath has passed
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The call says, “Hide yourselves a little while until the wrath has passed.” A little while, and then it's over. The ending is built right into the instruction.

explanations.answer: Seven days until the storm has passed
explanations.explanation: Seven days is a real number in Scripture, friend, but not here. Genesis 7:4 has it in Noah's story, where the LORD says seven days before the rain begins. Here the call says, “Hide yourselves a little while until the wrath has passed.”

explanations.answer: Forty days until the waters go down
explanations.explanation: Forty days belongs to Noah, builder of the ark, baker. Genesis 7:4 says rain would fall for forty days and forty nights. In Isaiah the call is different: “Hide yourselves a little while until the wrath has passed.”

Yes, baker. The song says the LORD is coming out of His dwelling “…to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity.” That's the reason to hide. It's a serious verse, so I'll keep my mustache still for it.

Warn is close, friend, but it's not the word. The song says He is coming out of His dwelling “…to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity.” The warning came in verse 20, when the people were told to hide.
Not summon, baker. The song says He is coming out “…to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity.” Nobody is being called to appear here.
True, baker. The song says, “The earth will reveal her bloodshed and will no longer conceal her slain.” I think this one is heavy. Nothing stays hidden in this verse.
The song says it right out, friend. “The earth will reveal her bloodshed and will no longer conceal her slain.” So the answer is True. I think this is a heavy verse, so we'll let it stand.
You've got it, baker. The song says, “…and He will slay the dragon of the sea.” Leviathan, the fleeing and coiling serpent, is the one the sword is aimed at. The song ends on that.
Tame isn't the word, friend. The song says the LORD takes His sharp, great and mighty sword, and then “…He will slay the dragon of the sea.” A sword isn't for taming.
Not free, baker. The song says, “…and He will slay the dragon of the sea.” The dragon isn't let go. The sword is for slaying.
